maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 15th day of November, 1935, between His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada and the government of the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, continuing my remarks on the motion before the house, I desire to place on record the percentage of reductions in the tariff on certain Canadian primary products entering the United States market. They are as follows: Live stock, 33i to 50 per cent: grass and clover seed, 50 per cent; turnips, 50 per cent; hay, 40per cent; live poultry, 50 per cent; dressed poultry, 40 per cent; leather, 20 per cent; lumber, 50 per cent.
One of the most important items in the entire pact is the concessions granted to the live stock industry, based on the average number of cattle slaughtered each year in the United States, which gives an estimated quota of approximately 227,700 head of Canadian cattle. While I agree that a larger quota would be desirable, a breakdown of the figures gives us the following result, provided that full advantage is taken of the quota. We have three major cattle markets in the Dominion of Canada-Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg. Divide the total quota by fifty-two, the number of weekly markets, and you get the number that may be shipped each week throughout the year from each of [DOT]these	markets.	It	means that 1,450
head of cattle may be shipped at the reduced rates to the United States from each of these three major markets throughout the entire year. I think that the average person who has a knowledge of market conditions as they affect the live stock industry must agree that during the last two or three years, with the congested condition that has affected the live stock markets of this dominion, if 1,450 head of cattle could have been lifted from each of our three major markets every week, a total of 4.350 head, it would have been of material benefit to our hard pressed live stock producers. I believe, sir, that the circumstances surrounding the cattle industry in this dominion for the last three or four years warrant some action being taken by the government to bring about a measure of relief, if possible, and I think we should be prepared to leave it to the judgment of the live stock industry of Canada to say whether or not this concession is of value to the industry.
There is one other point that I desire to emphasize, when trade declines, customs revenue declines, and then it is necessary to increase taxation or increase the debt, either of which places an additional burden on the people. I believe the increasing trade that will surely follow will relieve the Canadian taxpayer to some extent.
The reduced rates on imports have been criticized in some quarters, but they represent a measure of relief to the consumers of goods
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

in this dominion. There is one further point we must stress. The endorsement of a Canada-United States treaty does not weaken one thread in the bond that binds us to the mother country as the senior dominion in this commonwealth of British nations. Intraempire trade will remain the corner stone of the fiscal policy of the Liberal party, yet we must never lose sight of the importance of other potential world markets.
When I hear the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) ask, "Why could we not get the full fifty per cent reduction with respect to cattle and other commodities of that nature?" I realize why for a period of five years two and a half months the government under the leadership of the right hon. gentleman failed to negotiate a treaty with the United States. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) referred to the sales resistance which existed in connection with the marketing of Canada's wheat. After hearing the remarks of some hon. members and taking into consideration the fact that this treaty was not completed prior to the present administration coming into office, I am satisfied that there existed in certain quarters, and perhaps in the fiscal policy of the opposition, a trade resistance that reacted against the best interests of the primary producers of this dominion.
In conclusion, let me say that if the present government had followed the course advocated by the official opposition, they would have betrayed the trust placed in them by the electors of this dominion on October 14 last.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite gratifying to me to be able to remember and to look back on the many trade benefits that flowed from the passage of the first reciprocity agreement between Canada and the United States, sometimes known as the Elgin-Marcy reciprocity treaty, which died shortly after in 1866, a fact much regretted by the people of Canada as a whole. I remember also the great depression which followed thereafter, more prolonged and deepseated than anything Canada has seen since, with the exception of the one through which we are now struggling. With these thoughts still fresh in my memory, it is with considerable pleasure that I find myself after seventy long years, rejoicing with those who do rejoice at the birth of a second reciprocity treaty between Canada and the United States. But seventy years is a long time between trade liberation drinks with next door neighbours. Now that the government has turned its hand so auspiciously to

the removing of some of these trade fetters, let those of us who are like minded in this respect encourage, yea urge them on if necessary to greater feats in this direction. Possibly this joy and gratification I am experiencing is one of the compensating benefits which sometimes come with advancing years.
When I listened to the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who was followed by the booming support from Toronto and elsewhere, I was reminded of the fact that there was no opposition whatever to the first reciprocity treaty, which was in existence from 1854 to 1866. I have not the exact figures, but I believe in 1854 Canada was at least eighty per cent rural. At least that percentage of the population of Canada were in favour of reciprocal trade with the United States, and so far as I can find out there was really no opposition to the first agreement. Montreal, Toronto, the maritime provinces, Ontario, Quebec, all of Canada of that day, were in favour of this agreement. What has happened since then? The manufacturing industry in Canada was very primitive in 1854 but these interests have grown rapidly since then. It is quite natural that they should want to preserve Canada as a market for their manufactures by a stiff tariff which has enabled them to sell cheaper to foreigners than they do to their own people. They want it and the farmers do not want it, and there lies the difference.
After listening to our Conservative friends lauding this form of agreement with the United States for two years, I was quite anrnzed to see them loop the loop and vehemently attack this treaty. My first thought was that they had gone back on their former conversion, but when I come to think of it they never really were converted. They just wanted to give the people something that would distract their attention from their own shortcomings. I do not say that it is wrong to try to please the people, but it would have looked far more seemly if they had stayed with their new love for a little while. At least they should have supported the principle of this resolution. Surely it would not have torn their protectionist hearts asunder to have done that. They could have gone after the details as much as they liked, but they should have supported the principle. I am afraid their conversion at least was not like the conversion of Paul on the way to Damascus; possibly it more resembles Lot's wife when looking back on stricken Sodom.
I have no ill will against the Conservative party. We must have an opposition, and I should hate to see them commit political hari-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
kari by opposing this trade agreement. We do not know what would follow if another opposition took their place. I see a new party over there which has not yet won its spurs; they are strange to me and I still prefer even the Tory opposition to them as an opposition. We know what the Conservatives are and stand for, while the others so far belong largely to the unknown.
I am really at a loss to know how to explain the present attitude of the Conservative party. I have had many trimmings myself in my life and I know what it is to be defeated; I know what it is now to win, and I can therefore feel magnanimous. But even at this late day I would ask the Conservatives this question:	Would it not be more
logical for them to join with the government in support of this resolution? We do not need any further majority; we have in all conscience a large enough one now. But would it not be better for the house, would it not be more consistent on their part, would it not create a better feeling throughout the country for them to join with us in supporting this resolution than to put themselves in the position of having, so to speak, looped the loop so quickly with their newly adopted baby. In fact, I think it was a kidnap which they made from the Liberal nursery; but kidnapping is not as popular as it used to be and is much more dangerous -they found it dangerous. Their movement in the direction of reciprocity, never believed in by them, was made for the same purpose for which the wonderful radio addresses were given-to please the people. Of course, there is no great harm in that, but I think that propriety would have justified them in staying with the agreement, at least to the extent of supporting the principle of this resolution.
And now a word or two with regard to some of the amazing statements of the leader of the opposition. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) disposed most successfully of the more vulnerable parts of the right hon. gentleman's speech and I will now refer to the statement he made-it will be found in Hansard-that had it not been for the tariff increases against both the United States and Great Britain in 1930 there would have been no possibility of any kind of treaty in 1935 and 1936, History does not support that statement. At no time in the history of Canada did any party' ever enter into a reciprocity agreement, either with the United States or with Great Britain, after previously running the tariff up to a sky-high point of elevation in order to use that as a bargaining feature except the Conservative party in
1930, and what it did then did not work out as anticipated. If we are to give credit to the one who put up the tariff, on the ground stated by the leader of the opposition, then we might as well say that had it not been for that robber band in the eastern land who fell upon that historic traveller on his way from Jerusalem to Jericho, there would have been no story about the Good Samaritan and therefore we should give credit to the robber. We might as well say that as to say that had it not been for the high tariff devotee and addict who was at the helm of state in Canada in 1930 there would be no reciprocal agreement to-day. Of course that is nonsense.
I rather regret the necessity of having had to add these few words to an already prolonged debate, but I felt that it was my duty to speak because of the great importance of the question. We shall have a further opportunity of dealing with the subject, but I will conclude these few remarks by again expressing my appreciation of the action of the ministry in affording me an opportunity to see this day with its evidence, as revealed in this agreement, of returning sanity' and common sense with respect to questions of trade between nations whose interests are best promoted not by the erection of high and repelling tariffs and by other trade impediments, as if trade were some evil thing to be feverishly shunned instead of a great blessing to be pursued and sought after diligently. Rather should we trade as freely as possible, especially with our adjoining neighbour, consistent with our respective mutual interests and with the public revenue requirements of our own country.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I
always listen with a good deal of interest and amusement to the addresses of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who has just entertained the house with a brief jocular comment upon this trade agreement. He says he rejoices that after this long lapse of time separating agreements between Canada and the United States we are now about to consummate another. I cannot help thinking that my hon. friend's rejoicing must have a tinge of regret in it, namely, that between the years 1920 and 1930 no agreement of this kind was negotiated, nor were attempts made, as far as I know, to bring one about. Then he speaks about the tariff and seems to suggest that it is a harmful influence and that the protective principle in it is wrong. Well, all I have to do, I think, is to point out to him and to the members of this house that from 1896 until 1911 the protective
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

principle of the tariff was maintained by the Liberal party, and that between the years 1920 and 1930 the same principle was maintained by the same party.
He also thinks that we on this side would be well advised to join with the government in supporting this agreement. I know that advice was given in the kindliest spirit, but after all we have our responsibilities. We have our duty to perform, and I am siure he will agree that this is a question upon which there may be an honest difference of opinion. And looking back again I think that, in view of what has happened, my hon. friend must regret that in 1932 when there was before this house for ratification the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, which so largely extended and developed the trade of this country, particularly in the interests of the agriculturist, which my hon. friend with such ability always espouses-I say again that perhaps when he recalls the opposition of his party, including himself, to that agreement, there is a tinge of regret in his recollection.
I shall proceed to a consideration of this agreement. The trade agreement which is the subject of this debate has been before the people of Canada for some months, but it is only since the debate began in this house thai there has been that keen, critical analysis of it, that examination of its provisions, that will enable hon. members and the people of Canada to come to a conclusion as to its merits. As good citizens we all desire to approach any proposal for the extension of the trade of Canada with sympathy and with the desire to give approval wherever such approval can be given without damage to our agricultural and industrial development. At the same time we must keep alert for the purpose of discovering and if possible avoiding errors in connection with any attempted extension of our trade. We must be sure that we are getting a fair return for any advantages which we are extending to our neighbour, no matter how good that neighbour may be or how desirable it may be to extend our trade in every direction.
The historical review of the negotiations for trade with the United States has been made from two standpoints. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his very complete exposition of this agreement, traced back the development or lack of development of trade between Canada and the United States for a period of fifty years. He came to the conclusion that on the record the Liberal party were more favourable to development of trade in this direction than the Conservative party.
fMr. Stewart.]
But the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) supplemented the information given to the house by the Prime Minister and demonstrated, I believe beyond question, that the Conservative party had an equally honourable and equally favourable record in the matter of a disposition and a desire to extend our trade relations with the United States. Going back to confederation, to the declaration of the national policy, to the declarations of the Liberal leaders themselves, and looking at the matter from every standpoint, I think that honours in that direction are about even. I cannot understand how any member of the Conservative party at the present time, or any one who has been a member of it and is familiar with its traditions, familiar with its declarations of policy and the efforts it has made, can say that it has not been in favour of reciprocal trade relations with the United States.
Let us be fair about it. Both historic parties, and let me say all parties, recognize the value of trade and of markets for our products. No party has the monopoly in that respect. It would be strange indeed if any one party should have the exclusive possession of a disposition to trade, to extend our present markets and to develop new ones.
There are two great markets to which the Canadian people have always looked: one is in Great Britain and the other is in the United States. In both of those directions each of the two parties has made honest and sincere attempts to bring about favourable trade arrangements. The Liberal party endeavoured to bring about preferential trade, endeavoured to bring about a reciprocity agreement with the United States. Both parties failed, in large measure, until recently. The first outstanding success was that achieved by the late government, led by the present leader of the opposition, in the successful negotiation of the United Kingdom agreement. I say that was the first outstanding success, the first outstanding achievement in securing an extended market for Canada in the United Kingdom.
I do not desire to enlarge upon the results of the Canada-United Kingdom agreement. Any honest, fairminded citizen, looking back on conditions as they were in 1932, looking at the volume of trade at that time, and studying the statistics as they are now disclosed to us, must come to the conclusion that at a difficult time, a critical time, a time of great depression not only in Canada but all over the world, these agreements have been of significant advantage to the people of Canada. They deserved better support than they received in this house when they were before parliament

Canada-V. S. Trade Agreement
for approval, and they vindicated the faith and the vision of those who were responsible for their negotiation.
The basis of negotiations for the present agreement between Canada and the United States was prepared also by the former government. A change came about in conditions in the United States, a change, I think, of attitude of mind, a greater disposition on the part of the United States to trade more freely with Canada than she had showm during a period of ten years, particularly between 19(20 and 1930. I think we may truthfully say that that disposition to trade more generously with Canada was to a large extent due to the negotiation of the Canada-United Kingdom agreements. Be that as it may, there was undoubtedly a change in the attitude of the United States towards Canada, and, as soon as the president secured from congress authority to negotiate, the matter was taken up by the former government in earnest, a communication was presented, and from that time on negotiations proceeded. Upon the basis so laid, upon the opening thus made, this agreement-whether we agree with it in its conclusions or not-was undoubtedly founded.
There are many hon. gentlemen in this house who contend that the tariff policy of the Conservative party is one of extremely high tariffs. I am sure we have heard that throughout Canada, particularly in the last five years. If I had time I could put on Hansard a comparison and analysis of the tariff of Canada as compared with the tariffs of other countries, such as Germany, France, the United States and even Great Britain, and the tariff of Canada as compared with the tariffs of these other countries is not a high tariff. During the budget debate I hope to have an opportunity of developing this point a little further. A couple of years ago I spent some time on it, and I was pleased indeed to find, notwithstanding the allegations that the tariff policy of the Conservative party Tvas almost exclusive, that when compared with the tariffs of other countries that charge was not well founded. Undoubtedly during the depression, from 1929 to 1932 and 1934, measures were taken to increase the tariff, but the reason for these increases has been given. They were emergency measures, taken to preserve the financial integrity of the Dominion of Canada, and many who are [DOT]capable of judging the situation better than I are confident that if these measures had not been taken, disaster would have been the result.
Tariff increases have been made, and there is also a belief on the part of many hon. .members that if you increase the tariff you 12739-53
increase the cost of articles protected by the tariff. They believe on the other hand that if you would only reduce the tariff you would reduce the cost. Well, we have had a striking answer to that contention; recently in this house we had a debate on the price of agricultural implements, and during that debate the history of these prices over a period of years was reviewed. It has been shown by hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the house that a reduction in the tariff in more than one instance has resulted in an increase in the price. They are so convinced of the soundness of their theory that tariff increases always increase prices that now they are asking for an investigation to find out how it is that a reduction in the tariff has resulted in an increased price.
On entering into these negotiations with the United States, Mr. Speaker, I think we must keep in mind that the United States has certain undoubted advantages. In the first place it has a population of 120,000,000 people. I have heard hon. gentlemen on the other side contend that the United States presented an outstanding example of the success of free trade, that in that country we had the spectacle of 120,000,000 people trading freely between themselves. In the days of prosperity this was pointed to as a vindication of the policy of free trade. But what has happened? We find that in time of depression this great mass of people suffered just as severely as those countries that were not, in that happy position. I want to point out that the United States comes very close to obtaining the advantages of both free trade and protection. It has free trade between 120,000,000 people, but around that 120,000,000 people it has the advantage of a very high tariff wall. They have the advantage of cheap mass production; they have a climate favourable to the production of nearly all their own requirements, and at any and all times they are ready with a surplus of natural and manufactured products to export into the markets of the world.
We entered the negotiations under certain restricted conditions. Congress gave the President of the United States authority to negotiate trade agreements, but with the caution usually displayed by that nation they put certain restrictions upon him lest he might go too far. They said he could reduce the tariff, which was a high tariff, by only fifty per cent, that no article on the dutiable list should be placed on the free list, and that from the nations with whom he made agreements they must receive favoured nation treatment. There was also a limit of three years placed upon the life of such agreements.

speechtext: May I interrupt for just a moment? Does my hon. friend say he thinks we ought to get all that the president could have given under the powers congress granted? That would be a fifty per cent reduction on everything.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Yes, I would think so;
I would suggest that we should have got that. Canada gets concessions on cattle. I do not propose to deal with that matter, because there are others in the house more familiar with that trade than I am, but here is a quota which, as I understand it, limits our exports of cattle to the United States to approximately one in every hundred that are slaughtered in that country. Surely, with regard to only one per cent of their consumption, we might have expected our cattle to be allowed in free. In any case we get a reduction on cattle, to the value of 811,400,000. In connection with cream we also have a quota of 1,500,000 gallons, valued at $5,200,000. We get concessions on $2,300,000 worth of maple sugar; on seeds, $2,000,000; on other agricultural products, $4,200,000; on fish, $4,800,000; on lumber, $38,000,000; on minerals, $5,800,000; on whiskey, $82,000,000, and on miscellaneous commodities, $5,000,000, making total concessions of about $160,000,000 worth of trade. It is clear that the United States always liked our whiskey. They were short of it and needed our production, and it is possible that in any event they would have taken the quantity mentioned.
Then we get down to the items that are unchanged and upon which we get no concessions, but in respect of which a guarantee is given that there shall not be any increase in tariff during the life of the agreement.

First we have newsprint valued at $132,000,000; pulwood, $34,000,000; shingles, $20,000,000; minerals, $16,000,000; wheat, $8,400,000; fish, $4,000,000; chemicals, $8,200,000, and furs, $5,000,000, making a total of about $230,000,000. I should not like to dispute the value of having these commodities remain on the free list; undoubtedly that is an advantage. But in view of the fact that the United States had imposed a tariff on nearly all its imports, is it not fair to assume that having overlooked these items in the past they probably would have continued to allow them to remain on the free list irrespective of any agreement?
Let us see what Canada gives, as compared with what she gets. She gives concessions on oranges to the value of $21,000,000; fruits and vegetables, $11,000,000; canned meats, $3,000,000; corn, $8,000,000; other agricultural products, $4,000,000; farm implements, $40,000,000; machinery, $25,800,000; iron and steel, $15,700,000; household goods, $11,000,000; electric motors, $6,900,000; periodicals, $4,000,000, and other merchandise $16,000,000. The intermediate tariff is imposed upon textiles and clothing to the value of $24,800,000; furniture, $3,500,000; consumers' goods, $8,000,000; automobiles, $26,000,000; gasoline, $18,000.000; automobile parts, $56,000,000, and automobile engines, $11,700,000.
In connection with dairy products, in which I am particularly interested, I find that a rate of thirty-five cents per gallon still remains against Canadian cream, and the quota is limited to 1,500,000 gallons. I do not expect that this will be of very great advantage to the farmers of eastern Canada. The rate of five cents per pound on cheese is the same. When we remember that the domestic market of Canada consumes between eighty per cent and ninety per cent of these agricultural products, and that we are granting concessions upon fruits and vegetables, I think it is doubtful if there will be much advantage gained from these agreements by the farmers of eastern Canada.
The agreement has been defined as a step in the right direction. Before we make any decision I should like to know in which direction we are going. Is it a step in the direction of an adverse trade balance? If it is,, it is a step in the wrong direction. It is said that the agreement removes obstructions in channels of 'trade. Undoubtedly it removes obstructions in the channel of trade that will flow into Canada from the United States. It is said that it is an effort to destroy economic nationalism. Well, when 10,000,000 people start out to destroy the demon economic

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
nationalism they are undertaking a big task, and while we hope they may have some success I would be very careful about expecting too much in this direction.
The opinions of others as to the value to Canada of the trade agreement may be worth consideration. Without quoting in full I should like to refer to the comment of Professor Brebner, of Columbia university, which has already appeared on Hansard. In the United States there is a body of opinion that the agreement is perhaps more favourable to that country than it is to Canada. There is one feature of the agreement however to which I should like to refer briefly. May I draw the attention of hon. members to three articles in the agreement relating to its life, with special reference to duration and termination. Article XV is as follows:
The entire agreement shall come into force on the day of the exchange of the proclamation and ratification at Ottawa. The agreement shall remain in force until December 31, 1938, subject to the provisions of article VII, article X and article XIV.
Unless at least six months before December 31, 1938, the government of either country shall have given to the other government notice of intention to terminate the agreement on that date, the agreement shall remain in force thereafter, subject to the provisions of article VII, article X and article XIV, until six months from such time as the government of either country shall have given notice to the other government.
In other words the article states that the agreement shall remain in force for three years, and thereafter foe subject to six months' notice. Other significant articles must be read in conjunction with article XV. I shall refer first to article VII:
No prohibitions, import or customs quotas, import licences, or any other form of quantitative regulation, whether or not operated in connection with any agency of centralized control, shall be imposed by Canada on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of the United States of America enumerated and described in schedule I, nor by the United States of America on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of Canada enumerated and described in schedule II, except as specifically provided for in the said schedules.
Then follows the significant paragraph:
The foregoing provision shall not apply to quantitative restrictions in whatever form imposed by either country on the importation or sale of any article the growth, produce or manufacture of the other country in conjunction with governmental measures operating to regulate or control the production, market supply, or prices of like domestic articles, or tending to increase the labour costs of production of such articles. Whenever the government of either country proposes to establish or change any restriction authorized by this 12739-531
paragraph, it shall give notice thereof in writing to the other government and shall afford such other government an opportunity within thirty days after receipt of such notice to consult with it in respect of the proposed action; and if an agreement with respect thereto is not reached within thirty days following receipt of the aforesaid notice, the government which proposes to take such action shall be free to do so at any time thereafter, and the other government shall be free within fifteen days after such action is taken to terminate this agreement in its entirety on thirty days' written notice.
Article X reads:
In the event that a wide variation occurs in the rate of exchange between the currencies of Canada and the United States of America, the government of either country, if it considers the variation so substantial as to prejudice the industries or commerce of the country, shall be free to propose negotiations for the modification of this agreement; and if an agreement with respect thereto is not reached within thirty days following receipt of such proposal, the government making such proposal shall be free to terminate this agreement in its entirety on thirty days' written notice.
And article XIV;
The government of each country reserves the right to withdraw or to modify the concession granted on any article under this agreement, or to impose quantitative restrictions on any such article if, as a result of the extension of such concession to third countries, such countries obtain the major benefit of such concession and' in consequence thereof an unduly large increase in importations of such article takes place: Provided, that before the government of either country shall avail itself of the foregoing reservation, it shall give notice in writing to the other government of its intention to do so, and shall afford such other government an opportunity within thirty days after receipt of such notice to consult with it in respect of the proposed action and in respect of such compensatory modifications of the terms of the present agreement as may be appropriate; and if an agreement with respect thereto is not reached within thirty days following the receipt of the aforesaid notice, the government which proposes to take such action shall be free to do so at any time thereafter, and the other government shall be free within fifteen days after such action is taken to terminate this agreement in its entirety on thirty days' written notice.
There are three opportunities, Mr. Speaker, for the termination of this agreement, three avenues of escape, three doors of opportunity for terminating it. In view of the fact that there has been in the United States regulation and restriction under the NRA, which, although for the moment out of the picture, will probably be replaced by other legislation of the same effect, there are elements of danger and uncertainty and instability inherent in this agreement which make its termination almost probable, indeed which almost invite its termination on fifteen or thirty days' notice. I suggest that a com-
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

parison be made of the provisions for abrogation of this agreement with the relevant provisions of the United Kingdom agreement, which provide only for consultation.
I see that my time has almost expired, and I shall therefore summarize my objections to this agreement.
The agreement covers a long list of commodities, but on the whole, while it is broad in that respect, it is shallow in its concessions to Canada. Most of the rates of the United States tariff are still so high that little benefit will result. Many of our industrial plants will be forced to close, particularly United States branch factory plants. Unemployment with all its hardships will be increased; the investment of capital in industry in Canada will be discouraged; the home market, which absorbs from eighty to ninety per cent of our agricultural products, will be contracted because of decreased purchasing power at home; our railways will suffer decreased revenues because of the possibility of much freight coming in through ports other than our maritime ports. Let us remember this also, that when you import a ton of manufactured products from the United States or any other country our railways have just one hard of that ton, but if it is a ton of commodities manufactured in this country I am told that it represents the haulage of three or four or five tons of freight as against only one ton of a completely manufactured imported article. The development of this three or four or five tons is brought about through the assembling of raw material and everything that goes into the manufacture of the fininshed article.
In return for the concession we are granting to the United States of our intermediate tariff we should get a full fifty per cent reduction all along the line.
This agreement, I believe, will render it more difficult to renew and extend the provisions of the Canada-United Kingdom agreement. The agreement, the provisions for the termination of which I have already referred to, is limited in its life to three years, making its operation uncertain and almost inviting its termination. For these and other reasons which I propose to give more in detail when we come to deal with the different items, I shall vote against the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with pleasure to my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart). I have always liked him personally and I am not likely to change my mind after listening

to the rather effective speech which he delivered this afternoon on the wrong side of a very important question.
My hon. friend tells us that the Conservative party still has faith in protection, but faith without works is but a dead thing, and I wonder how many years they would go before their faith brought forth any fruit.
My hon. friend also tells us that the tariff does not always raise the price of a commodity, but there is a peculiar thing I might mention in this connection. I attended 175 tariff board hearings, and never once did I hear a manufacturer come before the tariff board and say: Will you please lower the tariff which I have enjoyed so that the price of the commodity I produce may be raised? Nor have I ever heard one say:	Will you
raise the tariff on the raw material which I use in order that I may get it at a lower price?
I want to suggest this to my hon. friend, who made some prophecies at the close of his address. He prophesied an increase in unemployment, a loss of revenue to the railways, and many other things. We are friends personally and I want him to invite me to his constituency for the next election. There the first thing I shall do, and I warn him now, is to look up Hansard and read the speech which he delivered this afternoon, and ask him how many of his prophecies have come true, i shall ask him at that time, when he will be prophesying some more, what is going to happen to his prophecies of 1940 or 1941, seeing that he prophesied so badly in 1936.
There is a rather peculiar mood in Toryism which I never can understand. The leaders suggest eternally upon every platform that we are always in danger when we trade with a nation larger than our own; that we are a nation of ten or eleven millions alongside a nation of 127 millions; and I often wonder how a unit of 127 millions manages to survive because it must trade with the world! Does anyone imagine that we would be better off if the United States should be towed away from its present moorings to-morrow and placed alongside the continent of Australia. I venture to say that we would lose many of the comforts and many of the enjoyments which we now have. We would lose the markets which we sorely need, and what would be a loss to Canada would certainly be Australia's gain.
Many strange doctrines have been brought forth by my hon. friends immediately to the left. One is that we have given away too much. A representative of the govern-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
ment which was in power in this country for five years and -which raised the tariff as high as it could possibly be raised, announces now that it was raised for the purpose of affording an opportunity for bargaining with other nations. But when a bargain is at last consummated by a new government, he tells the house, "You have given away everything; we have nothing left to give away!" When our taxes are reduced do we consider that we are giving away something or that we are getting something? I believe I have a sounder criticism to make of my hon. friends of my own political faith, and I intend to drive that home both here and throughout the country whenever I have an opportunity. My challenge to them is that they did not give away quite enough, that many of these tariffs are now atrociously high. The tariff on agricultural implements has been reduced from 25 per cent to 12} per cent. This is half what it was under the previous government, but it is still double what it was under their government which was in power in 1929 and 1930. I should like to give particulars of some of these reductions-permit me to put on my glasses so that I can give them exactly, because many of them are very small.
On February 6, 1935, the laid down cost ol artificial silk fabrics amounted to 83d per cent. On January 1, 1936, this cost was 73 per cent, but when the Liberals went out of power it was only 37} per cent. On cotton fabrics the rate has been reduced from 48} per cent to 42} per cent, but when the Liberals left office it was only 32} per cent. On cotton towels the total duty has been reduced from 60} per cent to 53} per cent, but in September, 1930, it was only 32} per cent. The laid down cost in February, 1935, of cut tobacco was 120 per cent; in January, 1936, it was also 120 per cent, but in September, 1930, it was 1024 per cent. There is another item here of particular interest at Christmas time. Our *Conservative friends raised the duty on toys coming from the United States from 32 per cent, as it was in September, 1930, to 53} per cent in February, 1935, and the Liberals have only had the good conscience to bring it down to 42} per cent. I would be quite willing to sacrifice at least two-thirds of this duty, and in doing that I do not think we would be doing too much.
There have been some gains, small though they may be. A friend of mine purchased a sprayer the other day and I wired him to find out what his saving had been. I received a wire in reply stating that the sprayer had been laid down at Burlington with a saving of $189. I submit that my friend Paul Fisher of Burlington who purchased this sprayer at
a saving of $189 does not think that anything of his has been given away. The Liberal party leaders have allied themselves with Paul Fisher in attempting to reduce his costs and improve the quality of the fruit which he grows by giving him a sprayer at a lower price. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for St, Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) ally themselves with the caterpillar and the codling, moth to destroy Paul Fisher's crop.
We have secured access to the American market for our cattle. I have a friend in my constituency who is a fairly large dealer la cattle. I had a letter from him the other day in which he says:
I have brought down from the west 400 head of cattle. We are feeding about 150 head, and with the feed so plentiful expect to have them in good shape. This U.S. deal has certainly helped us. When we go to Toronto with our cattle and the buyers turn us down, it makes them stand up and look when we have them billed to Buffalo.
I submit that by this agreement very material help is being given to our friends who are farming and who are endeavouring to make money by feeding cattle on the farms of Ontario. They now have two markets where formerly they had only one. I imagine that my hon. friend the Reconstruction party in this house, the hon. gentleman who was anxious that the farmers should have a little more, will be pleased with this one item by which we have given to the farmer a broader market and an increased opportunity to obtain higher prices.
We learn from our hon. friends on the Conservative side that we have done something deadly because we have endangered our balance of trade. I have said time and time again that more nonsense has been spoken in this house about balances of trade than about any other single matter. In regard to this I should like to point out that sometimes light does dawn on certain departments even if it does not spread to the head of the government. I have here a bulletin entitled Canada's Balance of International Payments, 1926-1932. I should like to read from the introductory paragraph as follows:
"Balance of trade" figures are frequently misinterpreted due to the persistence of an old doctrine long ago exploded that a nation's trade is in a healthy state when exports exceed imports necessitating an import of gold to make up the difference.
On the front of this pamphlet I see, " Published by authority of the Hon. H. H. Stevens, M.P., Minister of Trade and Commerce." Apparently there was not complete agreement between the Conservative party and the Reconstruction party even before they agreed

My hon. friend has also contended that when the Conservative party came into power in 1930 their first great task was to adjust the adverse balance of trade which existed in the exchanges between Canada and the United States. We know how often that sentence has been repeated, how often it has been explained; and therefore, my hon. friend said, the tariff had to be raised. They raised it, he said, at great cost and sacrifice to preserve the national integrity of this dominion. That is the essence of his remarks. Perhaps I had better quote his exact words, as reported at page 2394 of Hansard of April 26, 1932:
For, in the end, when you have more imports than exports an adjustment has to be made to bring about a favourable balance. If there is a gap it must be bridged, and it can be bridged only with fresh capital coming to this country or by borrowing.
In other words, when there is an adverse balance between Canada and the United States settlement has to be made by borrowing; and when we ceased to borrow in the United States in 1930, the decline in the adverse balance of trade between Canada and the United States absolutely and necessarily followed, and nothing could have prevented it following, no matter what government was in power, Liberal or Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or Social Credit. When our borrowing ceased in the United States, we had not then the means of payment; our imports from that country necessarily declined, and as a matter of course our adverse balance also declined.
And now let me show the decline in borrowings that took place. The total bond sales of the dominion in 1930, largely in the United States, amounted to $398,000,000. In 1934, according to the Monetary Times, our borrowings were $108,000,000. There was a decrease in bond sales of $290,000,000

$290,000,000 less with which to pay obligations in the United States; and as a direct consequence of that we had necessarily to reduce our imports, not because of action taken by the government but because we had not the means of paying.
I put it to hon. members on a personal basis. If any member has a salary of $5,000 and he has a capacity to borrow from his friends another $5,000, he may spend $10,000 in a year; but if his capacity to borrow is gone, he will cut expenditures and buy less. And that is what the nation did between 1930 and 1934. So much for the balance of trade.
My hon. friend makes this suggestion: the estimated loss of revenue through the agreement is $6,000,000. I am not going to dwell on that but I would point out that throughout Canadian and English history it not infrequently follows that a lowering of taxation increases revenue. We had that as far back as the days of Sir William Mulock in connection with postage, and it was repeated in the Robb budgets and in the budgets of Gladstone. In one particular instance, I may point out to the leader of the opposition as an example, the duty on blankets was doubled between 1930 and 1934, and the revenue fell off from $163,000 to $29,000. My right hon. friend raised the tariff on soups 7\ per cent, killed the imports, and we lost a revenue of $542,000. We know and realize full well that under a course of expanding trade, which the Liberals are now going to adopt, wherein we have made the first few faltering steps-and I wish they were stronger -we shall have an expansion of revenue just as we had on the previous occasion.
My hon. friend says that 82%o per cent of the value of all our agricultural production was used at home, and only 17A per cent of our agricultural production found a market abroad. My friend arrives at these statistics by taking the gross value of the agricultural production of Canada. The gross production is not the net production, because it includes the amount that is used up in the production of the net, for instance, feed for cattle and all the rest of that stuff which does not reach the market directly but enters it in the form of beef and other finished products. In that process some of these things are counted twice, and thereby he reaches a figure which is not more than one-half the total percentage of the exports of farm products.
I come now to a point upon which I wish to place some emphasis. It has been argued by almost everyone on the Conservative side of the house that this agreement will work great injury to our railways. We heard that from the hon. member for Leeds; we heard it from the leader of the opposition; we heard it from the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and, I think, from all the others who spoke against the resolution. Now, what is the test with regard to this question? I submit that it is the test of how it works out. In 1928-29 we had heavy -imports from the United States. What was the condition of our railways at that time? They were very prosperous; they were at the highest level of employment and the highest level of earnings in their history,

barring possibly the war years. So I thought I would work out a table giving the revenue of the railways, the index of that revenue, the imports from the United States, and the index of imports from the United States. Taking the basis of 1926 as 100 I find this in seven years, covering 1922, 1926, 1928, 1929, 1930, 1933, and 1934, the three highest years of railway revenue were the three years of the highest imports from the United States; the three lowest years of railway
revenue were years of the lowest imports from the United States. I find that when the Conservative government came into power, pledged as it was to cut down imports from the United States, it brought them down, and brought them down with a crash, but it brought the index of railway earnings down from 114 in 1928-as compared with 100 in 1926-to 54 in 1933.
