maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, shortly before recess an hon. member in the far corner asked a question which at that time was quite inaudible. Since then I have found that he asked why it was that Great Britain, a free trade country, was the first to feel the repercussions of the depression. His question contains a premise which is quite inaccurate

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Instead of being the first to feel the repercussions of the depression, Great Britain was the last. More than that, Great Britain departed less from the free trade principle than did the other great trading nations, and all through the depression suffered less than did the other countries of the world.
Before recess I was dealing with what had been said by some hon. gentlemen opposite, and in particular I was referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). He is very much concerned about some of our industries that he thinks will be adversely affected by the removal or reduction of tariffs between Canada and the United States. I remarked that he had stated to the house that if we wanted to know what some parts of this country thought about the great increases that had taken place in the tariff structure during the last five years we had simply to take note of the fact that nine Conservative members had been returned from Toronto and others from other industrial centres near by. He failed to look around the House of Commons and to see what the people of Canada thought about those increases in tariffs; he failed to recognize that Canadian consumers have a real interest in tariff structure.
All through the discussion hon. members opposite have been attempting to say that as a result of wider and freer trade some workmen are going to lose their jobs. Hon. gentlemen who use that argument have failed to recognize the fact that when imports have been greatest unemployment has been at its lowest point. That has been the case in all countries, and will continue to be so. I have been surprised to note that on all occasions when increased trade with the United States is suggested, hon. members opposite immediately get out the old flag and wave it in the breeze. I say that if they must use arguments of that kind, their arguments cannot be sound.
The world has gone mad with economic nationalism. This afternoon I quoted representative authorities from different countries of the world. I picked out only a few citations, but I have scores of them in which I read that the world will never be right again until we are prepared to support international trade on a wide scale. To-day in the United States there is a government prepared to deal with Canada. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) began dealing with that government, and went so far as to get some kind of understanding, just sufficient to use as a dummy to hang before the eyes of the electorate in an attempt to lead them to the conclusion that if the Conservative party were returned to power it w'ould require only one short step
to effect consummation of the agreement. But what do we find? Do we find hon. members opposite supporting the pact which they allege they framed? No, they do not; there are objections from all comers. As I stated before recess, we are thankful that the leader of the Liberal party had the support of Canadian people to an extent greater than that enjoyed by any former Prime Minister. He has gone to Washington and in a short time has consummated that pact. Is it perfect? I think not. I support the agreement, for what reasons? I support it because the principle behind it is that of providing greater facilities and more opportunity for international trade between Canada and the United States. I say that principle is sound. What is my objection to the agreement? My objection is that it does not go nearly far enough.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: It does not provide enough jobs.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I was gratified to hear in the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the statement that this is only a beginning, and that he hoped the present agreement would so commend itself to both countries that very soon there would be extensions of it. Let me say to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) that I am disappointed to find that in the agreement agricultural implements do not enjoy as low a tariff as they did under the famous May day budget of 1930. I suggest to the government that we should not be content until we go at least as far as the May day budget went in connection with agricultural implements. A few nights ago there was a discussion in this chamber concerning the increase of prices on agricultural implements. This afternoon the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) said that the increased price was the result of the lowering of the tariffs. I wonder if he believes that. I wonder if any member of the Conservative party believes it. I wonder if anybody believes it. The reason is, I think, quite different from the one suggested. If it is true that because of a reduction of tariff rates prices are increased, then why do we hear the arguments of hon. members opposite with regard to the reciprocity pact with the United States? They know perfectly well there is nothing in that suggestion.
What about automobiles? They now enjoy the intermediate tariff, yes. Have we gone far enough? I suggest that the Minister of Finance should look into the tariffs on automobiles, because the Canadian people have suffered long and severely the increased costs

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of cars purchased in Canada, a condition which must not be permitted longer to continue.
The agreement is good in that it is a beginning on the right path, and I trust that not only Canada and the United States but all countries of the world may get away from that intense economic nationalism which has prevailed. Some hon. members opposite have been wondering what was going to happen to the intermediate tariff. Their suggestion has been that if they knew what the Minister of Finance intended to do with the intermediate tariff they might vote for the agreement. I recognize that there may not be the same proportion between the various items under the intermediate tariff as there is under the general tariff, but if that is so my suggestion would be, not to correct this by an increase in the intermediate tariff, but that items in the general tariff be reduced so that those who might suffer slightly under the intermediate tariff in the agreement may obtain a relief through a reduction in the general tariff.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) asked the leader of the opposition a very pertinent question, namely, whether the right hon. gentleman opposite had suggested to the President of the United States that he would conclude an agreement provided the president would reduce the tariff in the United States to the full fifty per cent. Hon. members who were present will recollect that the right hon. gentleman did not give a direct reply. I have listened for several days to hon. members opposite jumping from pillar to post. They are not quite sure whether they should or should not support the pact.
Yes they are.
You are doing the jumping.

The hon. member will get a chance to vote on the agreement, but he has not spoken on it. I have listened day after day, and I noticed that they were not quite sure whether they would support the pact. Some were saying: "This is our baby, but since the other side has brought it into being and given it life, we do not think we can support it." I wonder where the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) will stand.
He will let you know after a while.

Where will he stand on the agreement when at least some of our primary products-not sufficient, but some-will gain

freer access to the United States? Where will the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Beaubier) stand? It is true that we are bringing goods into this country, but unless we recognize the principle that imports are paid for by exports, there could be no international trade.
Canada is behind the agreement; our people realize that it is in the interests of the consumers, and that it will bring benefits to many of our producers. If I felt that in future trade agreements we would go no farther than we have gone in this, I would not be satisfied, but I believe this is only a beginning. The government have demonstrated that they wish to trade with all other countries who are willing to trade with us on a reasonable and fair basis. This development of trade will bring comfort to many people in Canada who have been suffering m the last five years under exorbitant tariff and other restrictions greater than had been known previously. Those people will be greatly relieved to know that at last we are on the right road, and that we have in power a government which believes in international trade.
The debate has served this purpose if it has served no other. It shows this:	My
friends opposite really do not believe in international trade; that is the trouble. But hon. gentlemen on this side, members of the Liberal party, believe in freer intercourse in trade, and what can we expect from that freer intercourse? First, it will help the producer and the consumer. Next, it will help our railways. We hear a great deal about our tremendous railway problem, but hon. gentlemen opposite always put the cart before the horse when they discuss that problem. Unless we increase the business of Canada we shall never solve our railway problem. The best and the only way to solve our railway problem is to increase the volume of business done in this country, and then the railway problem will become a thing of the past. I support this bill whole-heartedly, not because it is perfect but because it is a step in the right direction, and I trust, Mr. Speaker, that we shall take many other steps of the same kind in the same direction, to free the channels of trade and let Canada return once more to that prosperity which she enjoyed, under a Liberal regime, from 1921 to 1930.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the country or the house is so very much interested in the history of what has been termed reciprocity nor do I think it is particularly interested in

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
who inaugurated the agreement which we have before us to-day. They are interested rather in just what it means to Canada.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite have intimated that it is just too bad the opposition are prolonging this debate, but if they will check up Hansard they will find quite a number of speeches similar to that delivered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Young), who has taken up a good deal of the time of the house but has not really discussed the items contained in this trade agreement.
I believe, as an hon. gentleman stated today, that the opposition play a part, and a very important one, in government. I have been in the house for ten years; I sat on both sides of it, and I always felt, when I was in opposition, that I was representing the people of a section of Canada, and that I was here to consider legislation and to help in solving the problems that come before us from time to time. Occupying a seat in the opposition to-day does not prevent me from supporting any measure which I think is likely to aid in solving any of thn difficult problems with which we are faced, and if this trade agreement would solve any of our problems, our unemployment, financial or other problems, I would support it wholeheartedly. I believe it is the duty of the opposition, not only to support good legislation, but to point out weaknesses in the legislation that is brought down in this house. I believe it is my duty, and I think it is the duty of every hon. member, to study and discuss this agreement. I have gone over the schedules carefully, but I must admit that it is impossible for any one member to decide whether this agreement is going to prove in the best interests of Canada as a whole. A member may know how it will affect his own particular part of the country, but I doubt whether any one member knows how it is going to affect every part of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
We have heard during the debate from members from different parts of this great country, discussing the details of this agreement and how it is going to affect their respective districts, and from that information the government will perhaps be able to size up the situation and correct the agreement in its details where that appears to be in the best interests of Canada. I think I am safe in saying that no member of this house is perfectly satisfied with the agreement as it stands. The previous speaker expressed himself in that sense. A number of hon. gentlemen opposite are dissatisfied with some of the items and with some of the changes that have been made in our tariff schedules by the agreement.
I said a moment ago that from the discussion that is taking place we can get a general picture of how this agreement is likely to affect the country as a whole. I listened with great interest last evening to the speech of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), who made it quite plain that this agreement would not help his section of the country; that it would not assist those fishermen in depressed circumstances who go down to the sea in ships, nor would it help the fruit and vegetable growers of that part of Canada. I also listened with interest to speakers from Ontario who pointed out the bad effects this agreement would have on certain branches of agriculture and also on the large manufacturing centres, where they expected the unemployment would be intensified rather than alleviated by this agreement. We have also heard from the members from western Canada, from the prairie provinces, who have made it plain that they endorse that part of the agreement which lowers the tariff on the implements of production. But we had in this house the other evening a debate on a resolution which I think made it clear that lowering the tariff does not necessarily lower the price of agricultural implements.
I wish, as one of the representatives from the great province of British Columbia, and in particular of that portion known as the lower mainland of that province, to take a few minutes to-night, to show how this agreement will affect the district which I have the honour to represent. We have there, in spite of what the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray-don) has said, perhaps one of the richest agricultural districts in the whole Dominion of Canada, comprising the dairy industry and all that goes with it; the poultry industry, perhaps the largest poultry plants in this dominion, and a large section that is devoted to production of fruit. In addition to agriculture, very large logging and lumbering operations are carried on in that district known as the lower mainland, there is also considerable mining development. So it is perhaps a typical district, and one which one would expect would be deeply interested in this agreement, not only because of the diversity of occupation that is carried on within its boundaries, but from the fact that it lies right up against the great state of Washington to the south and very close to the state of Oregon. The states of Washington and Oregon produce commodities similar to those produced in that particular part of British Colum-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
bia. It will thus be realized that anything which tends to reduce the tariff or in some cases to increase it, affects that particular part of the province. The states of Washington and Oregon have advantages over us, one of them being their climate. Their crops ripen earlier, this constituting a problem which we have to face.
I think the practical test of this agreement is: What do we get for what we give? I am going to consider it from that angle and as it affects that particular part of the country. What do we get? We get reductions in the tariff on cattle, on lumber and on whiskey. But there are limitations to these concessions. There is a quota on cattle and there is a quota on lumber. I believe the United States would have given us reductions on whiskey no matter what we did. The concessions granted in connection with cattle and lumber undoubtedly will be beneficial to these industries in British Columbia. I welcome anything that will help to restore the lumber and cattle markets which were lost under a previous Liberal government.
The United States tariff on beef cattle is reduced from three to two cents a pound for cattle weighing 700 pounds or over. But there is a quota limiting our sales to less than they were in 1929. In 1929, under the Fordney-McCumber tariff our cattle exports amounted to 247,000 head. Under this agreement our sales are limited to 155,799 head. So we are worse off than we were in 1929. On the other hand, on beef cattle entering this country, we are granting a reduction in the tariff of from three to two cents per pound. The tariff on sheep and lambs entering Canada has been reduced from S3 to S2 per head. The rate on live hogs has been reduced from three cents to one and a quarter cents per pound. We have reduced the Canadian tariff on fresh meats, beef, veal, lamb and mutton, from eight cents to six cents per pound. There has been a fifty per cent reduction on fresh pork, the rate being reduced from five cents to 2i cents per pound. Under this agreement bacon, hams and shoulders enter this country under a rate of 1J cents per pound instead of five cents per pound as was the case previously. By these items we will pay the price for the concessions which are granted in connection with cattle of 700 pounds and over.
What do the Americans say about this agreement? This has been quoted before, but I think it is worth while quoting again. Mr. Henry Wallace, Secretary of Agriculture, speaking at Chicago on December 10, last, is reported as follows:

It was his considered judgment that American agriculture gains from the Canadian reciprocal trade treaty so far outweigh the losses that the net advantage to our agriculture as a whole is very much worth while; that Canadian concessions on meats and meat products duties will open the way for our farmers to get back a bigger share of the British pork market. The new agreement will permit American pork to go to Canada to replace Canadian pork exported to Great Britain, thus, in effect, permitting increased exports of American pork to Great Britain.
The government has boasted that the dairy industry is receiving great benefits from this agreement. The American tariff on cream is reduced from fifty-six cents to thirty-five cents a gallon, but there is a quota provision. Under the Fordney-McCumber tariff it was twenty cents a gallon and in 1929 it was thirty cents a gallon, so we are worse off to-day than we were in 1929. The duty on milk has not been touched at all. The tariff on American butter coming into this country is reduced by two cents per pound. Nothing whatever has been done for the Canadian dairy industry.
Now, what about the reduction on lumber? Under this pact wTe are receiving a reduction of fifty per cent. While the charge against our lumber has been reduced to $2 per thousand feet, we are again met with a quota. The combined quota on Douglas fir and western hemlock is 250,000,000 board feet. Items 503 and 504 of our tariff permit similar lumber to enter Canada from the United States duty free. This reduction will help the lumber industry in our province and I heartily support anything that will tend to restore the American market for our lumber, a market which we lost in 1930 and in the years prior to that.
The Ottawa agreements have been assailed in this debate, but I want to remind the house that those agreements saved the lumber industry of this country. That industry in British Columbia wants once more to enter the markets of the United States, but it does not want to sacrifice for that concession the markets which it secured under the empire agreements. I think the lumber people are inclined to be alarmed at the continual sniping at those agreements by the Liberal party. Only the other evening the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) was reported on page 638 of Hansard, as follows:
The Liberal party was returned to power by a tremendous majority. The voice of the people spoke with no uncertain sound. That voice expressed discontent with existing conditions and with the policy of the previous administration. If there was any mandate at all in that vote of the Canadian people it was most emphatically a mandate that there should be substantial tariff reductions.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
The hon. member is also reported on page 637 as follows:
During the course of this debate mention has been made of the Ottawa agreements. I express the hope that never again will this country make an agreement along the lines and principles of the Ottawa agreements. I regard them as a dangerous step in the direction of economic imperialism.
What was the mandate of the Canadian people? As was pointed out in an earlier debate in the house, the mandate which the Liberal party received was received from thirty-five per cent of the people entitled to vote in the last elections. Does the hon. member consider that a mandate to destroy the empire agreements? There is to-day on the order paper a resolution moved by a Liberal member proposing that the trade agreements with the united kingdom be revoked. I say that the lumber people have a perfect right to be somewhat alarmed at this continual sniping by the Liberal party at these empire agreements.
Let us consider lumber under the Ottawa agreements. I have before me three tables giving the figures of lumber shipments from the Pacific coast for the last six and a half years; one table. Pacific coast to the world; another table, Pacific coast to the United Kingdom; and a third table, Pacific coast to Australia. These figures represent board feet and are from the Pacific lumber inspection bureau. I will not quote them in full, but as figures set forth, more plainly than hours of argument could, precisely what the Ottawa agreements did in the way of finding a market for this product of our province, I will give the figures for 1929 and 1934.
In 1929 British Columbia shipped to the world 399,000,000 feet; in 1934, two years after the agreements came into force, we shipped 830,000.000 feet. British Columbia increased' her shipments to the united, kingdom during the same period from 69 000,000 feet in 1929 to 455,000,000 feet in 1934, and she increased her shipments to Australia from 41,000.000 feet in 1929 to
128.000,000 feet in 1934. The result of the preference can be seen by a comparison of shipments from Washington and Oregon to the United Kingdom and Australia. During the same period, while our shipments increased enormously, shipments from the United States decreased correspondingly. For instance, in 1929 Washington shipped to the United Kingdom 196.000,000 feet, and in 1934 this was reduced to 28,000,000 feet. Oregon's shipments were reduced from 88.000,000 feet in 1929 to 8,000,000 feet in 1934.
These figures show what happened to the lumber trade of Washington and Oregon,
which did not have the Ottawa agreements to support them. It is well to remember that the Ottawa agreements were negotiated by the Bennett government and that when they were in this house for consideration they were opposed by every Liberal who then occupied a seat in the opposition. Let me put in concrete form what the Ottawa agreements did for the country at that time. In 1924 Canada held fifth place as an exporter to the united' kingdom. In 1930 we lost- so much of this business that she dropped to eleventh place. She slipped to twelfth place in 1931, jumped to fourth in 1932, the year the agreements were signed, and climbed to third place the next year. By the end of 1934 Canada took second place in the British market, headed only by the United States. That tells the story of the Ottawa agreements.
As I said at the beginning, there are in this agreement some good features and some that are not so good. This one and perhaps the one in regard to live stock will be appreciated by the people of British Columbia. But what price have we paid for what we have received? I have before me the opinion of Mr. Wallace, in a United Press dispatch from Washington dated November 19, which states:
In an official statement Secretary of State Henry A. Wallace said the treaty would benefit "the whole of agriculture" and predicted recovery of most of the $35,000,000 decline in United' States agricultural exports to Canada during the past five years. During that time, he said, exports to Canada of American farm products, upon which duty reductions are secured in the treaty, declined from $50,000,000 for the year ending March 31,	1930, to
$15,000,000 during the year ended March 31, 1935. Wallace cited the reductions granted to Canada on a quota limit of beef, cattle, calves and dairy cows and added:
"There are a few farm groups which will fear they are being hurt by the new agreement. but actually in those cases the tariff reductions are moderate, and in addition there are quota restrictions of such a nature that imports from Canada cannot affect the American price structure by more than 1 per cent. Both countries have made tariff concessions in order to increase the volume of trade between them. Canada has agreed to reduce import duties on a long list of American farm products, reductions ranging from 25 per cent on certain fruits and vegetables to 100 per cent on potatoes. The United States has agreed to reduce duties on seventeen Canadian farm products, and to bind the present rates by three others."
According to this statement Mr. Wallace is of opinion that the concessions given by Canada are quite valuable, and I notice he mentions potatoes. Under this agreement which we have before us-it has already been mentioned in this debate-potatoes are admitted free into Canada, while those of us
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

on the lower mainland of British Columbia, if we wish to export table potatoes to the United States, must meet a tariff of 815 a ton. I am told by producers in British Columbia that if this item is not restored to the general tariff rate, with the better climatic conditions in the great states to the south the producers of Washington and Oregon will be able to flood that part of Canada with potatoes at such a reduced price as to be less than the cost of producing in that section.
Another item in which we are very much interested, particularly in my district, is hay. In the duty on hay coming into Canada from the United States, we find a reduction of from 85 a ton to $1.75 a ton, while the duty on hay going into the United States is reduced from So to $3. I want to picture this to you, Mr. Speaker: This is a district lying close to a great state in the south producing an abundance of hay. I recall the time when hay was 83 a ton in the Canadian tariff. The Americans had a surplus and they established a selling agency in Vancouver. There was a string of trucks passing across the line, down through the lower mainland of the province, to Vancouver, passing by farmers' fields in which were piled tons upon tons of hay that they could not sell. The government five years ago raised that tariff to $5 and gave the farmers protection. What are those farmers to do now that the tariff is reduced to $1.75? The Americans under this agreement did not give us even the fifty per cent reduction; they reduced their duty to $3. The farmers of the lower mainland of British Columbia are much concerned over this item and some others as well.
What about the poultry industry? I have under my hand extracts, letters and telegrams, which I am not going to unload on Hansard.
I will say simply this, that there is a fear on the part of this industry in British Columbia that American eggs will enter in greater quantities, resulting in lower prices to the producer as a consequence of the reduction in duty from ten cents to five cents a dozen and the removal of the dumping duty. This is a serious matter to the poultry farmers in my part of the country. It means that protection from the dumping of American surplus eggs into Canada has been removed. I think there are some members in the house to-day who were here prior to 1930. They will recall the problem which faced the government of the day because of the large importations of eggs from the United States. In 1930, the last year of the low tariff, 3,000,000 dozen eggs were dumped into this country from the United States, with the result that this demoralized the Canadian market at certain seasons of the year. In 1934 importations

were reduced to 115,000 dozen. In 1934-1935 importations amounted to the paltry sum of approximately 817,000.
The poultry industry has had to overcome many difficulties in our province. One has been the price of feed, when we have had to compete with eggs marketed particularly during the summer season from other parts of Canada. With the protection that was afforded under the previous rate of ten cents-the total protection with the dumping duty amounted to about thirteen cents-they were able to stand the storm of the depression. Under the new arrangement, as I have pointed out, they will be called upon to face serious competition from the south.
Another product of the poultry industry is baby chicks. We have perhaps some of the largest plants producing baby chicks in the Dominion of Canada. One of the producers in my district has already this year received orders for 50,000 chicks. They have produced a very high laying strain in our part of the country. It will perhaps be recalled that hens from British Columbia secured world championships for a number of years. These producers went to a great deal of expense and much time and trouble to develop these high-producing flocks from which they market the baby chicks. Now, under this trade agreement we find that the protection which was afforded them during the last five years has been almost completely removed. The dumping duty is removed. One man writes informing me that in order to give protection that would put them on an equal basis with American producers it would be necessary that they should have a specific duty of at least seven to eight cents on each chick. They ask: What is a protection of twenty per cent against chicks imported from the great plants of California and Oregon? If they are laid down at the border at five cents apiece there is no protection.
Another industry which I mentioned was that of fruit growing. In this connection I want to refer particularly to what we call soft fruits. This is an important industry in the district which I have the honour to represent. Of one variety of fruit alone, namely strawberries, somewhere about 3,000,000 pounds were produced last year in the lower mainland of British Columbia. They were sold in carlots, in less than carlots, locally, and a large quantity was exported in processed form. Last year British Columbia shipped 153 cars of soft fruits out of the province, and in addition 700 tons of processed fruits were exported. The terms of this agreement provide for reductions in both the tariff and

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
the dumping duty. On vegetables the tariff was reduced from thirty to fifteen per cent, on fruits from twenty to fifteen per cent. Dumping duties are reduced by about one-fifth.
Take rhubarb for example. On rhubarb there is during the shipping season a reduction of 33y per cent. That is the reduction in the protection which was afforded that particular industry in 1935. On raspberries we have a reduction in protection of forty per cent. On strawberries the reduction is forty-four per cent; on prunes the reduction in total protection is thirty-three per cent; on pears, sixteen per cent; on apples, 28 J per cent. The protection on celery during the shipping season is reduced by sixty-one per cent. On asparagus we have a reduction of thirty per cent in the protection; and I can saloly say that asparagus growing is an industry that has grown up under protection; a large amount of money has been invested in it, and if it is not afforded proper protection it will be wiped out. As to the harm that this agreement will do to the fruit and vegetable industry, I might quote from my hon. friend the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), when he said the other night, that the harm would be considerably lessened if the government would use the power they have, if they would use that power in full, and if they would use it in time.
I have undertaken in a few minutes tonight to point out to the government what in this agreement I consider is not in the best interests of the people of the particular part of the country from which I come. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), as he has said that he has power to raise the intermediate tariff, that he exercise that power with regard to many of these agriculture items. They have been brought to the notice of the government during the last few days by members of this house. I should like to suggest that, for instance, in the case of potatoes the tariff be restored under the intermediate schedule; that the tariff on eggs be restored, also, if possible, that on baby chicks. As to fruit, as the member for Yale as well as I have said, the situation depends a great deal upon the production in those states to the south. If they have over-production; if they have a surplus which they want to dump some where, it will be necessary that we should have the very fullest protection, and that it should be applied in time. During my experience as representative of the district I have found that the difficulty, in dealing with matters pertaining to the application of 12739-55
dumping duties, has been to get them applied in time to give us proper protection during the shipping season.
I am sure that there are on the other side of the house members who are not exactly satisfied with every item contained in these schedules. I suggest to them that they, along with us of the opposition, urge upon the government the necessity of restoring this protection to these particular items which are so important to the agriculturists of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I was very much impressed with the striking point emphasized by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his address on this resolution. At page 503 of Hansard the right hon. gentleman said:
Let me stress this point-I have overlooked it up to the moment, but I want to emphasize it now. This government came back with a mandate from the people of Canada to put through a reciprocal agreement at the earliest possible moment. So far as asking the approval of this house is concerned, I regard that in some respects as an almost unnecessary step; the country itself has given so overwhelming an expression of approval of its confidence in a reciprocal agreement with the United States to be negotiated by a Liberal administration.
Agreeing so thoroughly with that view and believing as I did that this resolution was before the house bearing the approval of the people, I had not planned to participate in this debate. Within the last few days, however, what might be called challenges were thrown across the floor of the house by hon. members opposite. I think it was the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) who said, "Stand up. you maritimers, and express yourselves." That is why I have risen in my place here to-night. I am a maritimer representing the constituency of St. John-Albert, which includes the city of Saint John and boasts of the finest natural, year-round port in the Dominion of Canada. With all due respect to the other ports, we in the city of Saint John are modest when we make that statement, and we are prepared to stand by it.
This gives me an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to extend my most sincere congratulations to the right hon. Prime Minister upon having so successfully negotiated this agreement, and I want to tell him that I feel I am expressing the opinion of the people of the maritime provinces when I say that we are unanimously behind the agreement. Two of the greatest handicaps we have had to combat since the days of confederation have been discrimination in freight rates and in-



Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
ability to find a market for our natural products. I am happy to say here that, thanks to a Liberal government presided over by the present Prime Minister, the question of freight rates was partly solved by the introduction into this house of the Maritimes Freight Rates Act, and to-day we must again extend our thanks to the same government, presided over by the same able leader, for assisting us in solving our other difficulty of finding markets.
In 1927 parliament appointed a commission to inquire into the difficulties of the maritime provinces. That commission is now known as the Duncan commission. It was an able body of men, presided over by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, an eminent British statesman. That commission did its work and reported to this house. I have before me a copy of that report to which I intend to refer, because it is essential to the argument I have to present for the consideration of hon. members. May I say, however, that if hon. members will read the report they will find that this commission spent a great deal of its time in trying to solve the question of our freight rates, as well as in trying to develop some ways and means to help us in finding markets for our natural products. At page 31 of the report we have a reference to the maritime provinces with regard to primary industries. I want to bring these facts before the house so that hon. members may realize and understand that to-day we are faced with the problem of finding suitable markets for our products, but that problem has been solved to some extent and I am satisfied that when this agreement passes the house, the problem will be completely solved. At page 31 of the report of the commission I find the following:
Forest production for the year 1924 was thirty-five per cent of the total production of New Brunswick, seven per cent of that of Nova Scotia and four per cent of that of Prince Edward Island. Apart from the production of firewood, ties, rails, poles, posts, etc., for which no definite figures are available, the lumber industry consists, first, of the manufacture from raw materials produced by operations in the woods, of dressed lumber, or board measure lumber, laths and shingles, and, second, the manufacture of pulp and paper, an industry of comparatively recent development. The latter includes three forms of industrial activity: the operations in the forests with pulpwood as the product, the manufacture of pulp, and the manufacture of paper. The value of the output of lumber, laths and shingles manufactured in the maritime provinces 1924 was approximately $18,000,000, or over twelve per cent of the total value of such output in all Canada.... Fourteen pulp and paper mills operated in the maritime provinces in 1924. The average number of persons 
employed in the production of pulp was 15,000, and the capital invested in pulp mills and buildings was over $30,000,000.
The commission also dealt with the question of our fisheries, to which I should like to refer also:
The average yearly value of the catch in the maritime provinces during the five years from 1920 to 1924 inclusive, was approximately $16,000,000, or over thirty-six per cent of Canada's total catch during that period. During the year ending March 31, 1925, the capital invested in the maritime provinces in equipment for fishing, such as boats, nets, traps, and general gear, was over $12,000,000, or fifty-two per cent of the total capital invested in Canada in such equipment. The capital invested in factories and curing establishments was $5,500,000, or thirty per cent of the total amount invested in all Canada in such establishments. Thus the total investment in the fishing industry of the maritime provinces in primary operations and manufacturing was over $17,500,000, or forty per cent of the total Canadian investment in the fishing industry.
I refer to these facts because the commission found it necessary to bring before the house the proposition that the maritime provinces were concerned in the marketing development of their primary industries.
The agreement introduced by the Prime Minister contains certain provisions which are bound to prove advantageous to Canadian primary producers, and therefore must be highly beneficial to the maritime provinces. Can the agreement help the maritime provinces? If one examines the items in the schedule one would conclude that any man coming from the maritimes who did not rise in this house and support the agreement would not be true to his constituents.
I should like to quote no less an authority than Sir Thomas White, a former Minister of Finance and one who is by no means a Liberal. His opinions, however, are valued highly in regard to all matters affecting finance. After he had examined the trade agreement Sir Thomas expressed the following opinion:
The lowering of United' States tariff barriers on lumber, fish, agricultural products and other commodities should prove of material advantage to Canadian primary producers.
In this connection I shall quote, further, from an editorial which appears in the Saint John Daily Telegraph-Journal, one of the leading newspapers in the maritime provinces. It is an independent journal, and one which so far as I know has no political leanings.
Oh, oh.
The hon. member laughs; probably he is in the know, but I can tell him-

I think everybody knows.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

I am prepared to let him express his opinion, if he can speak as to the political bias of this paper. However I say that it is an independent paper, and in its issue of November 18, 1933, I find the following comment:
With reciprocity between Canada and the United States having practically unanimous support in this country, it carries an increased importance over that of any similar proposal in the past. There will be objections raised in many quarters to reductions in duties on various commodities effected, but so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, our real concern lies in the benefits which may accrue to those interested in primary products. With the wiping out of many maritime industries during the last sixty years, we may be pardoned if our symnathy wdth some manufacturing concerns has been somewhat lessened.
I shall now turn to a discussion of some of the items in the agreement. Speaking generally, I say that it is greatly to the advantage of the people in the maritimes. First, let us consider the situation with regard to lumber. Shortly after the federal elections I was deluged with requests from lumbermen in the maritime provinces urging me to take up with the government the matter of having United States customs duties reduced on lumber. I am sure similar requests came to the Prime Minister, because attached to the correspondence I received tvere copies of letters addressed to him. May I say to the hon. gentleman who refused to give me names last night that I can give them to him tonight, but shall be content by saying that the letters come from reputable lumbermen. They ask that the duty on lumber be cut at least in half. These representations were made to the Prime Minister, and that is exactly what they got. I say that any man from the maritime provinces could be accused of base ingratitude if he did not stand in his place and support the agreement, if for no reason other than the support it gives to the lumber industry.
Is lumber in quantities being shipped to the United States?

I would reply to the hon. member for Royal by stating that I have not the statistics before me, but I can assure him that just as soon as the agreement is fully ratified plenty of lumber will be shipped to the United States.
May I say that down in the maritime provinces we regard the report of the Duncan commission as more or less our magna charta. While I do not think it was within their powers to make representations as to the negotiation of treaties, by suggestion or inference the Duncan commission did make
12739-55^
such recommendations. Quoting from page 32 of the commission's report, which is available at the distribution office of the House of Commons, I find the following:
On the question of markets, witnesses who appeared before us from New Brunswick expressed the unanimous opinion that a trade treaty with the United States in respect of forest products would greatly benefit industry in the maritime provinces and result in extensive development.
The report states further:
The request made in this connection was supported by the Premier of New Brunswick on behalf of the province.
At that time the premier was the Hon. J. B. M. Baxter. He was a Conservative premier, and is now Chief Justice of New Brunswick. Sitting in the legislature at that time was the hon. member for Royal, who spoke last night in this chamber, and who applauded the premier when he appeared before the Duncan commission and made these representations. Now the hon. member appears in the House of Commons and listens to the leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett) oppose the agreement. We find the hon. member for Royal following the lead of his right hon. leader. Well, he may try to ride two horses, but when he goes back to New Brunswick I can assure him he had better not make the speech he made in this chamber last night for the benefit of hon. members assembled here in Ottawa.
. I now discuss the item of fish, one which is of prime importance to the people in the maritime provinces. In checking the schedule I find that the rate on halibut is reduced from two cents to one cent per pound, the rate on salmon from two to one and one-half cents per pound, and the rate on smoked herring from one and one-quarter cents to five-eighths cent per pound. There is the added assurance that lobsters and shell fish shall be kept on the free list for at least three years. These are matters of tremendous importance to the people in the maritimes. We in New Brunswick are deeply interested in the shipment of smoked herring, and the salmon industry, too, is of great importance.
Referring again to the Duncan report I find that the commission touched upon the question of finding markets for fish, and at page 33 of their report they state:
,, We shall deal with some other aspects of the fishing industry later.
Though in the case of fish, particularly cured hsh, we had considerable evidence to show the possib'hty of very greatly extending the market within Canada, representations were made to us, .as in the case of forest products, upon the desirability of a trade agreement with the United States.

That is the report of the Duncan commission, and I want to add that it is my belief that the introduction of this trade agreement is an implementing to some extent of the report of the Duncan commission, and I commend the right hon. the Prime Minister for the splendid work he has done in negotiating this agreement.
I could go on all down the line and speak of the benefits that will accrue to the maritime provinces from this agreement. The duty on seed potatoes, for instance, from March to November, has been cut from seventy-five to forty cents per hundredweight, and while there is a quota of 780,000 bushels, that is three times the amount of the current exportation, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister himself. The duty on turnips has been reduced from twenty-five cents to 121 cents per hundredweight, and the duty on maple sugar from six to four cents per pound. In that one item alone of maple sugar I can see tremendous possibilities for my own province of New Brunswick.
It is only recently that the Telegraph-Journal, the paper which I mentioned a moment ago, had a leading editorial urging the people of New Brunswick to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by the trade agreement. There is no question that this agreement contains provisions which are of great advantage to the people of the maritime provinces. Some may say: Well, you did not get all you wanted or all you asked for. But, Mr. Speaker, this world is so constituted that we shall never get all we want, and I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) realizes that to-day. But is there any reason why any member from the maritime provinces, at any rate, should vote on the floor of the house against this agreement which means so much to the people of the maritimes?
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) quoted last night from two. newspapers published in Carleton county, New Brunswick, and read a letter from a gentleman who lives in that county. The tenor of those reports in the papers was that the potato industry would be injured as a result of putting American potatoes on the free list, but I would remind the house that those editorials, coming fro-m Conservative newspapers, were more or less inspired, and that the gentleman who was referred to last night was the editor of one of those newspapers and Conservative organizer for the county.
I want to correct the hon. gentleman. One of those newspapers is a strong Liberal paper.

I would say to the hon. member for Royal that I have reference to Mr. Hatfield whose name was quoted here last night. Turning back to the question of potatoes, which seems to agitate the mind of my hon. friend-
And some others too.

Well, if those hon. gentlemen would take the trouble to check the statistics they would find that nothing has happened yet under this agreement to injure the potato industry of this country, because in the month of January of this year there was shipped into Canada only 381 hundredweight of American potatoes as compared with 202 hundredweight in 1935, or in other words an importation of the value of S600 for the whole dominion.
But what is going to happen in 1936?

I have just given the importations for January, 1936. I have made a further check on the potatoes coming in within the last two months; I find that nothing but cull potatoes have been coming in, and I believe there is a sinister motive behind that importation. The speeches we have heard from the Conservative side of the house on the question of potatoes dealt only in generalities. They have produced no facts and figures to show that the potato industry will be injured as a result of American potatoes being put on the free list. It is all right to talk generalities, but let them give us the facts. I am giving the facts because the figures I have given came from the Department of National Revenue in Ottawa only a short time ago. I do say this, however, that within the next few months American potatoes will no doubt come in as they did in the past,

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
at a time when we have no potatoes to compete with them. In June, 1935, for instance, 57,466 hundredweight of American potatoes were shipped into Canada, and in July, 15,870 hundredweight. But as soon as our own potatoes were available and we were able to compete, shipments from the United States fell off. We need have no fear that the Canadian potato producer will not be able to meet the competition of American producers at all times because we grow a superior potato.
In conclusion, I would just say that it almost takes one's breath away to hear our friends opposite expressing fears for the success of our great national ports, when we remember the experience we have had in the last five years, with trade restrictions such as they have been, and the business of our ports falling off alarmingly. I repeat, it almost takes one's breath away to find these new champions springing now to the rescue of our national ports.
I have before me some statistics supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce. They show that in 1929, the last full year in which the Liberal party was in power, inward shipments of sea-going vessels arriving at St. John amounted to $15,691,713, whereas in 1934, the last full year in which the Conservative parly was in power, those shipments had dropped to $8,113,477. The figures for 1929 show that goods exported from St. John were valued at $55,861,050, whereas in 1934 they dropped to $33,209,104. It may be said that values do not offer a true criterion by which to make comparisons; that the true test is tonnage. In order to be absolutely fair, I shall give the figures in tons. The official figures show that in 1929 the amount of freight imported through Saint John totalled 387,050 tons, whereas in 1934 the figure had dropped to 350.854 tons. Exports amounted to 1,075,765 tons in 1929, whereas in 1934 only 515,164 tons were exported. These figures show how shipping fell off at the port of Saint John due to the trade agreements negotiated by the last government. The records of other ports will show a somewhat similar condition.
When the late government introduced a tariff measure affecting Cuban sugar, the government of Cuba retaliated and raised their tariff against our potatoes. This meant the loss of the sale of some 3,000,000 bushels of potatoes per annum. When we were making these potato shipments to Cuba there were something like four ships leaving Saint John every week for that country. Employment was given to the dock workers and our railways were assisted by the traffic. After the tariff on Cuban sugar had been raised by the
leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) we had scarcely one boat sailing from Saint John. When hon. friends opposite set themselves up as the champions of the ports, I want to tell them that we would rather leave our fate in the hands of the government presiding over affairs to-day. It will be the salvation of our ports when this agreement is put into effect and there will be further benefits when the trade agreement with Japan is in force. Other agreements are to be negotiated which will open up the markets of the world and our ports will have the advantage of increased traffic.
I am proud to record my vote in the house in support of this measure. This will be my first vote on a major measure in this chamber and I am thankful to know it will be for an agreement between Canada and the United States which means so much to our maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard quite a number of speeches on this agreement, some of them very interesting and all of them varied in character. Just before six o'clock the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) said that he thought sufficient members had been heard from. I do not believe he can criticize the Conservatives from Saskatchwan for prolonging this debate. I think I should have the privilege of making a few observations and I can promise the hon. member that there will be only one Conservative voice from that province.
Much has been said about international trading and we have been accused of pursuing a policy of economic imperialism. This matter has been viewed also from the standpoint of domestic markets. I am not going to discuss this matter from any of those different angles, but I shall refer briefly to international trading. I admit that international trade is a splendid thing, but I would remind hon. members that when the government headed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came into power in 1930, Canada was in eleventh or twelfth position as far as international trade was concerned. When that government left office the position of Canada had been materially improved because of the policies pursued, this country being then in either fifth or sixth position.
Many hon. members have discussed this matter from a local viewpoint, and this is quite natural as they are interested in how this agreement may affect the part of the country they happen to represent. I am also going to deal with the question from that standpoint. The right hon. leader of the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
opposition has reviewed the history of reciprocal trade or reciprocity since confederation and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) also made a careful review of the policy of reciprocity. I have nothing to say in that regard other than to remind the house that when Sir John A. Macdonald introduced his national policy in 1878 he announced that it provided for free trade with the United States on a large number of articles. As was made quite clear by the leader of the opposition, since that time the Conservative party has always been ready to negotiate with the United States agreements along reciprocal lines as long as they were fair and equitable and did not sacrifice the interests of the Canadian people.
I should like to review briefly what has taken place in the United States with respect to tariffs. I mention first the Wilson-Underwood tariff which was in effect from 1913 to 1921. This tariff made substantial reductions in the duty on a considerable number of articles. I hold in my hand a list of forty odd primary products that were affected. All grades of cattle, hogs, sheep were allowed free entry under that tariff. All kinds of meat products such as beef, fresh and frozen, pork, fresh and frozen, and salted pork, were all free. Dairy products were free with the exception of butter on which was a duty of 2J cents per pound. Then followed a long list of grains and seeds which were all free. We next had the Ford-ney-McCumber tariff which was introduced in 1922 and which commenced an era of protection in the United States. Heavy rates of duty were imposed upon certain Canadian farm products and the result was a great reduction in the sales of these articles in the United States. That tariff was in force until 1930 when the Hawley-Smoot tariff came into effect. No matter what the Prime Minister said with respect to wider markets and freer trade, he was powerless to prevent the increase in tariffs from going into effect in the United States.
Then we had in June, 1930, the Hawley-Smoot tariff which completely closed the door against the entry of Canada's primary products into that country. Those were the words used by the Prime Minister when discussing that tariff; he said that it completely closed the door. But he made no protest. The statement he made at that time has already been put on Hansard during this debate. I could give the list of some forty primary products with the duties which the Hawley-Smoot tariff imposed-and they are very considerable-but I will not take time to go into the details. Suffice it to say that fMr. E. E. Perley.]
that tariff placed heavy duties on cattle, poultry, fruits, vegetables, grains of all kinds, pork and pork products, and dairy products generally. The real effect of the Hawley-Smoot tariff was not felt in Canada until after the change of government in 1930, when it turned back to the Canadian market a great flow of our primary products that had been going into the United States prior to the coming into effect of that tariff.
Then we come to the United Kingdom agreements consummated in 1932. The Bennett government negotiated these agreements, which turned into the United Kingdom a considerable volume of trade that had formerly been going into the United States. I think it is important to point out that by 1934 we had witnessed the result of the United Kingdom agreement. It was the turning point; it was the turning point so far as the President of the United States and their government were concerned; it brought them to the position in which they were prepared to negotiate a reciprocal trade arrangement with Canada. I think that is important.
It is not necessary for me now to review the negotiations leading up to the signing of this agreement. That ground has been so thoroughly covered by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition that I do not deem it necessary to comment upon it. What is the effect of a reduction in duties? I think the house will agree with me that a reduction in duties has really two effects, the first being an increase in the volume of imports-at least that should be the first effect-and then the displacement of home labour by foreign or outside labour. And here I want to be fair. I think the government speakers could have taken advantage of an argument with respect to these two effects, though I have not heard it mentioned. However, I will state it. In a fair trade agreement these effects would be counterbalanced by provisions for greater exports which in turn would absorb the labour disturbed by imports. That is a fair conclusion. But can one find in this agreement provisions that make for that counterbalancing effect? I cannot.
This agreement, like all others, is in some respects good and in other respects bad. I will refer briefly to certain products in which Saskatchewan is more or less interested. The question of potatoes has been mentioned on both sides. We do not export potatoes from Saskatchewan to any great extent; very few, if any, are exported. But if it were possible, under this or any other agreement, for eastern Canada and the maritimes to sell their potatoes

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
to our good friends to the south, we might be induced in the west to grow potatoes and ship them to Ontario and Quebec, so that these two central provinces might know what real potatoes are. I have not had a real potato since coming to Ottawa; I say that with all due respect to my good friend from Toronto, and I have told him so. Conservative members from Manitoba and Saskatchewan are going to bring their own potatoes here and have a few baked in the restaurant.
I come now to dairy products. This is important. I have searched the agreement and cannot find in it very much for the dairy producer in Canada. There is no lowering of duty on milk, milk powder, butter or cheese. It is true there is a reduction on cream from fifty-six cents to thirty-five cents a gallon, but there is a quota of 1,500,000 gallons which is only half the amount of cream exported to the United States in 1929, prior to the Hawley-Smoot tariff coming into effect. It may be urged that we in the prairies do not export cream or milk. That is quite true. We cannot make cheese advantageously on account of the distances between farms; they make cheese in eastern Canada. They can export cream and milk from eastern Canada to the states immediately to the south, but we cannot do that in Saskatchewan. But I will say for the benefit of hon. members that in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta we can make butter second to none produced in any part of this country; and if an arrangement could be made whereby the maritimes and eastern Canada could obtain a market to the south for their dairy products we could supply the east with the best butter produced in Canada. I have under my hand some figures showing the number of prizes taken in 1935 at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto. The three prairie provinces secured 1,406 prizes and Ontario and Quebec together secured 174. That was for butter alone.
I should like to put on the record figures to show the exports of butter and dairy products from Canada to the United States in 1929; that is, before the Hawley-Smoot tariff took effect. In that year we exported 3,750,000 gallons of sweet milk; 1,000,000 pounds of milk powder; 2,833,000 gallons of cream; 7,411,000 pounds of cheese; 231,000 pounds of butter, and the same year we exported 7,213,700 pounds of bacon and 240,000 head of cattle. I think that shows the importance of the dairy industry. And there is in this agreement, other than what relates to cream, nothing that will help us to sell a pound of dairy products in the country to the south.
Let us take cattle. The reduction is one cent per pound on cattle over 700 pounds.
I admit that is beneficial. The farmers of western Canada were very glad to see it. But I think we might have had the full cent and a half, representing the fifty per cent which the United States president could have given. However I do not think the item will be of any benefit; owing to the quota we shall not ship very many more than we did in 1935, before this agreement came into effect. The decrease which has already occurred in the price, with the increased freight rate, more than counterbalances the one cent per pound reduction in duty. I have on my desk letters which I have received from Saskatchewan farmers who were shippers of cattle and who expected to ship more, but when they compare prices they dare not take a chance. Here, again, we have a quota. Cattle have been spoken about so much during the debate that I almost hesitate to mention the matter. But the quota, which will be in the neighbourhood of 230,000 head, is equal only to the average of what we shipped in the years 1927, 1928 and 1929. I want to draw attention to the fact that there is no reduction for the class from 175 to 700 pounds which is commonly spoken of as stockers and feeders. Also, the restriction surrounding the exportation of the milch cow is such that I do not think the farmers will take advantage of it because, as I understand the situation, there has to be a clear bill of health as far as tuberculosis is concerned for at least a year before the cow is exported.
At this point I want to reply to a statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) with respect to this one cent per pound on cattle. I may say that it is rather an advantage for us to have the hon. gentleman in parliament when he speaks for himself, because we know that in the last parliament he had a mouthpiece in the person of Mr. Young, the then member for Weyburn. I believe Mr. Young put forth free trade views even better than the hon. gentleman can. The hon. member made the statement this afternoon that the one cent per pound arrangement was very favourably received by cattlemen or certain friends of his in Ontario. He said that he had a friend in Ontario who had so much feed last fall that he bought and brought down 400 head of western cattle; that he put 150 head in the feed lot, and when he shipped the finished cattle to Toronto, if the price did not suit he could then bill them through to Buffalo.
Now, why did he not tell the whole story? He said how pleased his friend was when he found that he had the advantage of shipping them to Buffalo at a cent a pound reduction in duty. Well, this is the story as he should

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
have told it. He said that he got these cattle from western Canada. Last fall the prairie farmers, the farmers out in Saskatchewan, were short of feed. We know how the calamity that occurred there last year affected our crops. Many of them had to sacrifice their cattle. Not having the feed, they could not properly finish their cattle to take advantage of the one cent per pound reduction in duty by shipping them to the south. I may say that these must have been a class of cattle which were feeders or stockers; they certainly were not fit for the market or they would not have gone into the feed lot in Ontario. They would be in a class not included under this agreement. If all grades of cattle had been included, they would have gone to St. Paul or some other point south from Saskatchewan. However, they came down to Ontario, and he got cheap freight; when they go into the feed lot they enjoy the cheap freight and a through billing. What he really was doing was exploiting the poor western farmer again. That is just what happened. I should like my hon. friend to make that speech out in Saskatchewan and tell the farmers there how, owing to this agreement, they were able to do that with western cattle.
I ask hon. members opposite:	What is
there in this agreement, when you boil it down that is of any value to cattlemen, and what is there in it for the grain grower? Is there included in the agreement any grain that will go into the United States or that we can ship under a lower rate of duty? And how about the dairy producer? These, I think, are all questions that should have been answered.
Much has been said about lumber. I am all in favour of a reduction that gives an entry into the United States for lumber. One of the members from British Columbia has elaborated to-night on that; it has meant certain benefits from a reduction in the duty; but I want to point out that already I have received protests from farmers in Saskatchewan owing to the fact that since the first of the year there has been an increase of $2 per thousand feet on lumber. The farmers out there are not receiving this very kindly. During the last five or six years they have not been able to buy lumber to repair their houses, their barns, their granaries and so on, owing to the calamity they have met in the loss of crops. They are in a similar position as regards lumber as they are in regard to machinery; the old machines are worn out and they have to buy new. And now, since the first of the year, they are faced with an increase of S2 per thousand feet of lumber, 
and they are also faced with a considerable increase in the price of machinery.
The reduction of duty on implements is from twenty-five per cent to 12i per cent. When first the news came out, it was heralded as a great accomplishment on the part of the present government. The farmers received it very kindly because they expected to get their implements cheaper to the extent of at least twelve per cent of duty. But when the prices came out on February 1 and they found there was an increase from $2 to about S40 per implement, as the case might be, this was not very favourably received. Protests have been coming in, as we know; I have them before me, along with quotations from the western press to the effect that the farmers have protested. We know what has taken place in this house in the last two days, that a committee has been appointed to investigate this increase.
The fact remains, no matter how much we hear about free trade and about what lower tariffs will do, that when, on different occasions, we have had reductions in the tariff on implements in Canada, every time this has meant an increase in price, and that when we have had increases in the tariff, this has meant a reduction in the price. That is something I cannot figure out, and it has not been figured out by any of the members opposite. There is a joker somewhere. But I would remind this house that when the leader of the opposition was in power and we raised the duty on agricultural implements coming into Canada, he made the manufacturers put their name on the dotted line that there would not be any increase, and if the present Prime Minister had had the courage to talk to the manufacturers in Canada there is no doubt that there would not have been the increase now that they have lowered the duty.
Is my hon. friend in favour of taking the whole duty off agricultural implements?

Well, if it will work the way it has worked during the last four years, that when the duty was increased we had lower prices and when the duty was taken off we had increased prices,
I would say no, for that one particular item.
What difference does the price make if you do not pay for your goods?

Well, I think the implement manufacturers have been pretty well paid in the past. If they got

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
half of what 'they sold their implements for they would have been pretty well paid. However, that is the fact, and we shall see what will happen when we have the investigation. I am just as anxious to know as is any other member of this house. I am sure that the farmers of the west want to know, and if we can do so we should solve this problem of why these prices have gone up when the duty has 'been lowered.
I have tried to cover most of our primary products in a fair way and to point out the advantages, but there are one or two distinct disadvantages as well. Reference has been made already to the reduction in duty on pork and pork products, a reduction from five cents to lj cents in some grades and from five cents to three cents in other grades.
I should like to tell the house what the secretary of 'the United States Department of Agriculture thinks about this item of pork products. He stated:

there would be a wide market in Canada for United States pork. He could see Canadian pork going to Great Britain and United States pork taking its place in Canada.
I have before me the figures with regard to exports of pork from Canada and imports of pork from the United States. In the last five years we imported from the United States 33.309,509 pounds and exported to that country 15,827,800 pounds. For the last three years or so exports and imports have practically balanced, but during that period we have had a very considerable increase in our exports of pork products to the united kingdom under the Ottawa agreements, under which we have a quota of 280,000.000 pounds of bacon. In the first year during which the agreements were in operation we secured in the united 'kingdom a market for some
43,000,000 pounds of bacon. In the second year we exported about 60,000,000 pounds and last year we exported over 80,000,000 pounds. I would remind the house of the statement made by Mr. McLean of Canada Packers, before the price spreads committee, that during the first year the agreements were in operation they meant 826,000,000 to the hog producers of Canada. In that year our exports amounted to only 43,000.000 pounds, so that on a similar basis that market must have been worth from $35,000,000 to $40,000,000 last year. Compare what the Ottawa agreements meant to the hog producers with the statement made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) the other night, that this agreement would mean $18,000,000 to the cattle growers of Canada. It must be remembered that in making that statement the hon. member assumed that all 'the cattle produced in
Canada during the year would reap the benefit of the $9 per head, which was the figure he used. That, of course, would be utterly impossible, but even if it were not, when these two advantages are weighed I think everyone will agree that the balance is in favour of retaining the hog market.
Now I should like to quote one or two opinions in connection with this agreement. This afternoon the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) also quoted the opinions of various people. First, I should like to quote a gentleman whose opinion I know the government will not hesitate a moment in accepting. I refer to a statement made by Grant Dexter, which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post in January of this year:
The United States treaty has undermined the foundations upon which the Ottawa treaties were built.
I think that is something important which should be remembered. The other opinion I wish to mention is that of the President of the United States, contained in an address to the American Farm Bureau at Chicago on December 9, 1935, appearing in the Duluth Herald of the same date:
Agriculture, far from being crucified by this agreement, as some have told you, actually gains from it. We export more agricultural products to Canada than we have imported from her. We shall continue to do so, for the very simple reason that the United States, with its larger area of agricultural lands, its more varied climate and its vastly greater population produces far more of most agricultural products, includin'"1 animal products, vegetables and fruits, than does Canada. In the case of the few reductions that have been made, quota limitations are set on the amount that may be brought in at the lower rates.
That is an important statement, and we should keep it in mind. Then the president continued:
On the other side of the picture we believe, and most unbiased men believe, that the general increase in our trade with Canada, including the exports of our factories, will so add to the purchasing power of hundreds of thousands of wage earners that they will be able to spend far more than they do to-day for the products of our own farms, our own forests and our own fisheries. Greater trade is merely another word for more production and more employment. The proof of this particular pudding is in the eating, the best way to judge the new accord is to observe how it works out.
That is certainly good advice.
It will be impossible for me to conclude my remarks to-night, Mr. Speaker, so I will move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
